newsitem.title: NIGERIA: U.N. puts Nigeria under human rights spotlight.
newsitem.headline: U.N. puts Nigeria under human rights spotlight.

text.p: Nigeria will come under sharper scrutiny over alleged human rights abuses after the appointment of a special United Nations investigator for the African nation, diplomats and activists said on Wednesday.

The military government of General Sani Abacha is yet to comment on a meeting of the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva on Tuesday which appointed a special investigator to probe allegations of major rights abuses in Nigeria, including arbitrary detentions and executions.

In the resolution adopted by the 53-member forum, it also called on the Abuja government to guarantee fundamental freedoms and release "all prisoners, trade union leaders, human rights advocates and journalists currently detained".

"It is the worst sanction any nation can get from the U.N. human rights commission," said Clement Nwankwo, executive director of the Constitutional Rights Project, a leading human rights lobby group in Nigeria.
"We welcome the vote completely given the fact that the government has shown no sign of change to improve its human rights record," he added.
The vote was 28 states in favour of the resolution, six states against with 19 abstentions. Nigeria is not a member at this year's Commission, which has a rotating membership.
Other local human rights activists expressed similar sentiment, saying the vote had put Nigeria in the league of pariah nations such as Burma, Iran and Iraq.
The U.N. human rights forum had been widely expected to censure Nigeria at the Geneva forum.

But Western diplomats in Lagos who followed the proceedings said the overwhelming vote in favour of the European Union sponsored resolution showed Abacha's government had to act quickly to show the international community that it was serious about democratic and human rights reforms.
"Nigeria can not continue to keep quiet about allegations of human rights abuse and expect they will go away," a diplomat said.
Africa's most populous nation of 100 million is shunned by the West over a 1993 annulment of a presidential election that was to have restored democracy.
Since then many people have been detained including Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the vote.
He was detained in 1994 for proclaiming himself president and was last seen in public in August 1994 when he was charged with treason in a trial stalled on legal technicalities.

Nigeria's international standing worsened further in 1995 when author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other members of his Movement for the Survival of Ogoni Peoples (MOSOP) were hanged for the murder of four Ogoni chiefs in a trial questioned worldwide as unfair.
MOSOP was predictably the first group to hail the Geneva decision to appoint the human rights investigator.

"The vote is a clear indication that the international community has chosen to pitch its tent with the suffering people of Nigeria, including the peace-loving people of Ogoniland in Nigeria who have been under military siege since the judicial murder of Ken Saro-Wiwa and either other members of MOSOP in November 1995," MOSOP said in a statement issued in London.
Nineteen Ogoni youths are still in detention over the same charges that Saro Wiwa faced.

Two U.N. rapporteurs who should have visited Nigeria before the Geneva session called for the appointment of the special investigator in a report they wrote after stopping a planned visit to Nigeria in a row with Abuja over access to detainees.

The government chief human rights official Awwal Yadudu criticised their report, saying in his statement at the Geneva forum published by local newspapers on Wednesday that "events in Nigeria have been deliberately misrepresented and exaggerated".
